# Exact depth for three unequal interval fibers

This note proves a sharp theorem for precisely three consecutive positive interval fibers. It is a gluing benchmark and does not resolve arbitrary mixed dimension.

## 1. Statement and normalization

Let a convex body in R times R have exactly the three positive fibers at integer bases -1,0,1, with endpoint lengths 0<a<=b and middle length U. In this note there are no other nonempty integer fibers. A map (z,x)->(z,x-alpha z-beta) centers both endpoint intervals. It preserves the lattice times R, one-dimensional fiber measure, and the entire ambient halfspace family. Reflection of the base exchanges the endpoints if necessary. The normalized fibers are

    K_-=[-a/2,a/2],  K_0=[s-U/2,s+U/2],  K_+=[-b/2,b/2].

Convexity implies, and is equivalent for the convex hull of these three fibers to,

    U>=(a+b)/2,       |s|<=U/2-(a+b)/4.                 (1)

Indeed the only extra section imposed at base zero by the two endpoint fibers is their Minkowski average [-(a+b)/4,(a+b)/4]. Every point of the convex hull at base zero is a convex combination of that average and the specified middle interval. Thus containment proves equality of the specified and actual sections. The convex hull is a compact full-dimensional body, and its integer base projection is exactly {-1,0,1}.

Write D(x) for absolute (unnormalized) ambient halfspace depth at (0,x), and F=max_(x in K_0) D(x). Define

    g(x)=min{a,max{0,(a+b)/2-2x}}.                       (2)

Then

    D(x)=min{U/2+s-x+g(x), U/2-s+x+g(-x)}.              (3)

Writing sigma=|s|, its maximum is

    F=U/2+a,                          sigma<=(b-a)/4;
      U/2-sigma/2+(b+7a)/8, (b-a)/4<=sigma<=(b+3a)/4;
      (U+a)/2,                        sigma>=(b+3a)/4.  (4)

The global absolute maximum over the actual mixed-integer set is max{b/2,F}. Consequently the smallest possible normalized maximum depth, among all such bodies with endpoint ratio r=a/b fixed, is

    B(r)=1/(4-2r),                 0<r<=1/5;
         (1+5r)/(6(1+r)),          1/5<=r<=1/3;
         (1+3r)/(4+6r),            1/3<=r<=1.           (5)

Every value is attained. It is strictly greater than 1/4 for positive r, tends to 1/4 as r decreases to zero, and equals 2/5 at r=1.

## 2. Minimizing every oblique endpoint cap

For an interval of length c centered at zero, the mass above threshold t is

    f_c(t)=min{c,max{0,c/2-t}}.

For a halfspace through (0,x) with positive continuous normal normalized to one, the endpoint thresholds t_- and t_+ obey t_-+t_+=2x. Conversely every finite pair satisfying this equation comes from an ambient oblique halfspace. We claim

    inf_(t_-+t_+=2x) [f_a(t_-)+f_b(t_+)]=g(x).          (6)

Put c=(a+b)/2-2x. If both caps have mass strictly between zero and their full interval lengths, their sum is c. If one cap is full, the sum is at least a. If both are empty, their threshold sum is at least (a+b)/2, so c<=0. If the smaller-interval cap is empty and the other is proper, t_->=a/2 implies the other mass is at least c; the same argument applies with the roles reversed. These cases prove that the sum is at least min{a,max{0,c}}. If c<=0, take both thresholds at or above their upper endpoints with the required sum. If 0<=c<=a, take t_-=a/2 and t_+=b/2-c, giving masses zero and c. If c>=a, make the smaller interval full and the larger empty by taking t_+ sufficiently large and t_-=2x-t_+. These are finite thresholds. This proves (6), including every full/empty transition.

The middle mass of such a cap is U/2+s-x for x in its interval. Reversing the continuous normal gives the other expression in (3). A vertical halfspace containing (0,x) contains the middle fiber and at least one endpoint, so its mass is at least U+a. The minimum of the two expressions in (3) is at most their mean, at most U/2+a. Therefore vertical halfspaces cannot lower (3). Any containing halfspace can be moved to pass through the candidate, decreasing its intersection, so this computation includes all closed ambient halfspaces. Boundary points of each nonvertical interval cap have zero one-dimensional measure; vertical caps were handled directly and retain their full boundary fiber mass.

## 3. A single exact maximizing point

In (3), the first expression is continuous and strictly decreasing in x, while the second is continuous and strictly increasing. At the lower middle endpoint x=s-U/2, condition (1) gives x<=-(a+b)/4, hence g(-x)=0; the second expression is zero. At the upper endpoint the first expression is zero. There is a unique crossing, and it is the unique middle maximizer.

Reflection x->-x lets us assume s>=0. At x=0 the first expression minus the second is 2s, so the crossing is nonnegative. For x>=0 one has g(-x)=a. Solving the crossing in the three branches of g gives respectively

    x_*=s,                   s<=(b-a)/4;
        s/2+(b-a)/8,         (b-a)/4<=s<=(b+3a)/4;
        s-a/2,               s>=(b+3a)/4.              (7)

Each branch condition is exactly the condition that the displayed x_* belongs to that branch of g. The preceding endpoint sign and uniqueness argument shows x_* belongs to the middle interval. Substitution into the increasing expression gives (4). For negative s, reflect the point in (7).

At either exposed endpoint base, the mixed depth at any point is exactly its ordinary interval depth. One inequality follows by retaining the own fiber. For the other, take any own cap and choose a finite base tilt large enough to exclude both other bounded fibers. Thus the endpoint maximum depths are a/2 and b/2, proving the global formula.

## 4. Optimizing placement and middle length exactly

For fixed a,b,U, formula (4) is nonincreasing in sigma. The worst placement is therefore the largest permitted sigma,

    sigma=U/2-(a+b)/4.

Substitution yields

    F_w(U)=U/2+a,       (a+b)/2<=U<=b;
           (U+b)/4+a,   b<=U<=b+2a;
           (U+a)/2,     U>=b+2a.                    (8)

We minimize max{b/2,F_w(U)}/(a+b+U). The scale b cancels, so set b=1 and a=r. In the first range, the two numerators cross at U=1-2r. This crossing lies in the first range exactly when r<=1/5. Before it the quotient is decreasing; after it the derivative is (1-r)/(2(1+r+U)^2)>=0. For r>=1/5 the first-range minimum is at its left endpoint. In the middle range F_w exceeds b/2, and the derivative of the quotient is -3r/(4(1+r+U)^2)<0. In the third range the derivative is 1/(2(1+r+U)^2)>0. Hence the only candidates are

    1/(4-2r) at U=1-2r,                    r<=1/5;
    (1+5r)/(6(1+r)) at U=(1+r)/2,           r>=1/5;
    (1+3r)/(4+6r) at U=1+2r,               all r.

For r<=1/5, the third candidate minus the first has positive numerator 2r(2-3r). For r>=1/5, the third candidate minus the second has numerator 2(1-3r)(1+2r). All denominators are positive. These comparisons prove (5). Choosing the listed U and the extremal placement in (1), then taking the convex hull construction from Section 1, proves attainment.

The three expressions in (5) agree at their shared endpoints. Their derivatives are positive on their respective ranges. Their exact excesses above 1/4 are

    r/(8-4r),  (7r-1)/(12(1+r)),  3r/(8+12r),

respectively, all strictly positive on the stated ranges. This proves the final assertions.

## 5. Scope and boundary cases

This auxiliary theorem assumes three positive one-dimensional fibers and a,b>0. No zero-dimensional Hausdorff measure, vanished endpoint, additional boundary-only integer fiber, or higher-dimensional body is silently included. The limit r->0 is a limit of the exact formula, not an assertion that its proof applies unchanged to a different intrinsic measure. The shear and reflections above have absolute continuous-fiber Jacobian one and preserve the mixed-integer set; setting b=1 in the scalar optimization simply divides every length by b, which cancels from the normalized ratio. The maximizing point is a single point on one of the three actual integer fibers. No graph-depth substitution occurs.

The accompanying rational verifier checks the piecewise formulas, all finite cap-breakpoint minima, maximizing-point identities, and extremizing parameters over a finite grid. It is an arithmetic diagnostic; Sections 1--4 provide the general proof.
